query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Targeted interfacial doping of eutectic high-entropy alloys with a boundary‐segregating element (e.g., a carefully chosen dopant capable of lowering interfacial energy) will strengthen and toughen the internal lamellar colony interfaces. This modification reduces microcrack initiation, thereby improving both room-temperature tensile strength and ductility compared to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies containing numerous pristine internal boundaries that are prone to microcracking under tensile loads.
generation.intervention: Apply a targeted interfacial doping/coating process by adding a dopant element known to segregate at internal boundaries during alloy processing.
generation.structural_mediator: Modified internal boundaries within the lamellar colonies where the dopant segregates, enhancing interfacial cohesion and toughness.
generation.mechanism: The dopant is expected to preferentially segregate at the numerous lamellar colony interfaces, lowering their energy and making them tougher. This enhanced interfacial robustness reduces the likelihood of microcrack initiation and propagation, allowing for better load transfer and sustained dislocation activity, which together improve both tensile strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline eutectic HEA without interfacial doping, the doped alloy should exhibit higher tensile strength and improved room-temperature ductility due to reduced microcracking along its internal boundaries.
generation.baseline: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with conventional, untreated dual-phase lamellar colonies that display a trade-off of high strength with limited ductility due to microcrack initiation at the untreated interfaces.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected within the specific microstructural regime of dual-phase lamellar colonies. The intervention’s success depends on achieving an optimal dopant concentration and uniform distribution at the interfaces; excessive doping or a different microstructural morphology may negate these benefits.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal choice of the dopant element, its concentration, and the processing conditions required to achieve uniform interfacial segregation remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of eutectic HEA samples: one set modified with the targeted interfacial dopant and one unmodified control group. Conduct detailed microstructural characterization (e.g., transmission electron microscopy and atom probe tomography) to confirm dopant segregation at internal boundaries. Perform room-temperature tensile tests to measure tensile strength and ductility, and use in-situ imaging (e.g., high-speed optical or electron microscopy) to monitor microcrack initiation and propagation.
measurements: Quantitative assessment of tensile strength and elongation at failure
Interfacial chemistry and dopant distribution (using TEM/APT)
Microcrack density and propagation rates during deformation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the interfacial doped samples do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility, or if the microcrack initiation behavior remains unchanged compared to the control group, then the hypothesis that targeted interfacial doping improves both strength and ductility is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

High strength and ductility, often mutually exclusive properties of a structural material, are also responsible for damage tolerance. At low temperatures, due to high surface energy, single element metallic nanowires such as Ag usually transform into a more preferred phase via nucleation and propagation of partial dislocation through the nanowire, enabling superplasticity. In high entropy alloy (HEA) CoNiCrFeMn nanowires, the motion of the partial dislocation is hindered by the friction due to difference in the lattice parameter of the constituent atoms which is responsible for the hardening and lowering the ductility. In this study, we have examined the temperature-dependent superplasticity of single component Ag and multicomponent CoNiCrFeMn HEA nanowires using molecular dynamics simulations. The results demonstrate that Ag nanowires exhibit apparent temperature-dependent superplasticity at cryogenic temperature due to (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation behavior. Interestingly, HEA nanowires can perform exceptional strength-ductility trade-offs at cryogenic temperatures.
